newsitem.title: INDIA: RBI dollar buying pushes Indian rupee down.
newsitem.headline: RBI dollar buying pushes Indian rupee down.

text.p: The Indian rupee weakened on dollar purchases by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to end Tuesday at 35.87/88 per dollar against the day's opening 35.830/835, dealers said.
They said the RBI bought dollars in substantial amounts from 35.835 rupees onwards to 35.875.
Dealers said the rupee traded in a narrow range between 35.83 and 35.84 per dollar till early afternoon when the RBI hit the market and pushed the Indian currency down.
"It was bound to happen," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Yesterday's 35.83/84 levels were artificial and largely the result of speculative action."
He said the rupee ended Monday higher at 35.825/835 against the opening 35.87/90 because banks unwound speculative long dollar positions, built up ahead of the budget.
Dealers said the rupee weakened despite dollar selling by a large eastern-India based state-run bank.
"The RBI was mopping up the state-run bank's dollar supplies," said one dealer. "Had these (dollars) come to the market, the rupee could have moved up...maybe past 35.80."
He said the rupee would now return to last week's range.
"We should see the rupee back to a 35.87 to 35.90 per dollar range," he said.
Dealers said premia on forward dollars ended marginally down on Tuesday.
"Rates came down as a big term lending financial institution was selling forward dollars in the near months," said a dealer.
"A large state-run bank sold September dollars," he added.
The annualised premia on six-month dollars ended Tuesday at 6.52 percent against Monday's close of 6.59, dealers said.

Dealers said they expected premia to remain at current levels with a possible rise in mid-March when domestic liquidity is expected to tighten as companies make tax payments ahead of the end of the financial year on March 31.
"Call money rates are expected to harden by mid-March," said a dealer. "We may then see forward premia also go up."
"Further banks also seem to be short on forward dollars. Rates could rise when they square their positions."
